Nutrition Therapy that helps:
1. *Amino Acids Therapy:* In a study of malnourished patients with COPD, increasing protein and energy intake for 3 months by providing a powdered protein (preferably *EAA*)-and-energy supplement each day resulted in improved nutritional status, greater respiratory muscle and handgrip strength, less fatigability of respiratory and skeletal muscles, and less breathlessness. The target goals for total daily protein intake were 90 g for men and 80 g for women. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3057956/ 
*Whey Protein* can be included for those who tolerate dairy & tolerate lactose & don't have any autoimmune conditions. Whey contains gamma-glutamylcysteine, which is a pre cursor for glutathione synthesis. Although cells cannot take up glutathione, gamma-glutamylcysteine is readily trans ported into cells, where it combines with glycine to form glutathione. In a case report, a woman experienced marked 
improvement in lung function while consuming a whey based protein supplement. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10713031/
2. *NAC* as @919920895552 mam suggested  at a dose of *600 mg/day* has been shown to enhance the clearance of mucus by the pulmonary cilia in healthy volunteers who had a slow baseline clearance rate.
3. *Magnesium* (600 - 800 mg/d)
4. *Potassium*: The mean potassium concentration in skeletal muscle biopsy samples was 14% lower in COPD patients than in matched controls. In COPD patients receiving diuretics, the mean muscle potassium concentration was 27% lower than in controls. In contrast, serum potassium levels did not differ between COPD patients and controls. These findings indicate that patients with COPD may have intra cellular potassium depletion despite normal serum potassium levels. Potassium deficiency may contribute to muscle weakness and fatigue in these patients. An increase in potassium intake may therefore be useful for some patients with COPD.
5. *Phosphorus*: Of 158 patients hospitalized with COPD, 21.5% had hypophosphatemia (serum phosphorus < 2.5 mg/dl). 91% of the patients with hypophosphatemia had a defect in renal phosphate reabsorption. This defect was associated with the use of specific COPD medications that are known to influence renal phosphate handling: xanthine derivatives, glucocorticoids, loop diuretics, and beta-2 adrenergic bronchodilators. If the patient has low serum phosphorus levels switching to non-phosphorus depleting medications should be considered when possible. 
6. *Vitamin A* (If low): Vitamin A plays a role in maintaining the cells of the alveolar epithelium, and may also help prevent the development of respiratory tract infections. In a double-blind trial, supplementation with a relatively small dose of vitamin A *(3,300 IU/day)* for 30 days significantly improved measures of pulmonary function. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8942419/ 
7. *L Carnitine*: In short-term double-blind trials, supplementation with 4-6 g/day of L-carnitine for 1-2 weeks increased the capacity of COPD patients to tolerate a rehabilitation program (exercise training of the diaphragm and upper body). In addition, supplementation with *2 g/day* of L-carnitine for 6 weeks increased exercise tolerance and inspiratory muscle strength in COPD patients. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3137180/ 
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16612469/

9. *Buffered Vitamin C* (500-1000 mg/d) for 1 to 2 months.
10. *Glutathione by inhalation:* Cigarette smoke is known to deplete glutathione in the airways by irreversibly degrading it to glutathione-aldehyde derivatives. Glutathione can be delivered by aerosol directly to the lungs and it remains fully functional as an antioxidant when administered by that route. In case reports, 6 of 7 patients with COPD experienced an improvement in breathing after treatment with nebulized glutathione. The dosage was 2 ml twice a day of a solution containing 60 mg/ml of glutathione. The solution was nebulized and inhaled over a period of 5-10 minutes. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11056412/
Glutathione should not be given to patients with sulfite sensitivity, because glutathione in aqueous solution exists in equilibrium with sulfites and may therefore induce bronchospasm in sensitive individuals.

16/04/2025, 15:56 - +91 89563 56280: *What is an elemental diet?*

An elemental diet is a type of medical nutrition therapy consisting of *pre-digested nutrients* that are easily absorbed in the small intestine. It is often used to support people with digestive disorders, malabsorption issues, or those who need gut rest.

Diet consists of liquid meal replacement formulated with pre-digested nutrients. 

This means that the:

* Proteins - are broken down into amino acids or short peptides
* Carbohydrates - are broken down into simple sugars
* Fats - are in the form of medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) for rapid absorption
* *Zero fiber* , making it gentle on the inflamed gut

Such formulas usually come in liquid or powder form, are easy to digest and nutritionally complete.

*Mechanisms of Action: Why Does It Work?*

1. *Reduces digestive burden* : Nutrients are pre-digested; hence GI tract does not need to take effort to break down food. This allows the intestinal lining to "rest" and heal.

2. *Starves Pathogenic Overgrowths* : Absorption occurs early in the small intestine & fewer nutrients reach the distal gut, where bacterial overgrowth thrives. 

3. *Minimizes Antigenic Load* : Elemental diets are hypoallergenic, eliminating common dietary triggers.

4. *Corrects Malabsorption & Nutritional Deficiencies* :The rapid absorption of elemental nutrients helps patients regain nutritional status.

*Who Can Benefit From an Elemental Diet?*

* Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO)
* Eosinophilic esophagitis
* Crohn’s disease
* Ulcerative colitis
* Cancer
* Radiation-induced diarrhea

*Duration & Transition Back to Whole Foods*

Elemental diets are used for shorter periods (2-6 weeks) for acute flare management. After improvement, whole foods are gradually reintroduced while monitoring for intolerances. <This message was edited>
